title: Applet Programming III – HTML Hosting & Applet Tag

mcqs.question: What does HTML stand for?

options.B: HighText Machine Language

mcqs.explanation:
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language — the standard markup language for creating web pages. It uses tags like , ,

,

to structure content. Browsers interpret HTML to render web pages.

mcqs.question: Which HTML tag embeds a Java applet into a web page?

options.B: <applet>

mcqs.explanation: <applet code='MyApplet.class' width=300 height=300></applet> embeds a Java applet. The 'code' attribute specifies the .class file. Width and height specify the display dimensions in pixels. This tag was the standard way to embed Java applets in HTML pages.

mcqs.question: Which attributes are mandatory in the <applet> tag?

options.B: name, size

mcqs.explanation: code (the .class file name), width, and height are mandatory. Without code, the browser doesn't know what to load. Without width/height, it doesn't know how large to display the applet. Example: <applet code='App.class' width='400' height='300'>

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of the HTML <head> tag?

options.B: Contains metadata like the page title, shown in the browser tab

mcqs.explanation: <head> contains metadata: <title> (browser tab title), <meta> tags, <link> for CSS, <script> for JavaScript. It's not visible in the page body. <title> inside <head> sets what appears in the browser's title bar/tab.

mcqs.question: What does the HTML <body> tag contain?

options.B: The visible content of the web page — text, images, links, applets

mcqs.explanation:
contains everything visible on the web page: text, headings (

), paragraphs (

), images (), links (), tables, and applets (). The tag goes inside .

mcqs.question: What does the <h1> HTML tag create?

options.B: A large heading (header level 1)

mcqs.explanation:
creates the largest heading (heading level 1). Headings go from

(largest) to

(smallest). Example:

Welcome

displays 'Welcome' in a large, bold font. Used for page titles and section headers.

mcqs.question: What does the HTML <a> tag create?

options.B: A hyperlink to another page or resource

mcqs.explanation: Click here creates a hyperlink. The href attribute specifies the destination URL. Clicking the text 'Click here' navigates to the URL. stands for 'anchor'.

mcqs.question: What HTML tag displays an image?
mcqs.explanation: displays an image. src specifies the image file path. alt provides alternative text (accessibility, shown if image fails to load). Example: .

mcqs.question: How are comments written in HTML?

options.B: /* comment */

mcqs.explanation: <!-- This is a comment --> creates an HTML comment. Comments are not displayed by the browser but are visible in the page source. Useful for documentation and temporarily disabling code sections.

mcqs.question: What do <b> and <i> HTML tags do?

options.B: <b> = bold text, <i> = italic text

mcqs.explanation: text renders text in bold. text renders text in italic. Combined: bold italic. Modern HTML prefers (bold) and (italic) for semantic meaning, but and are still widely used.

mcqs.question: How is the <applet> tag structured with parameters?

options.B: <applet code='App.class' width=300 height=300><param name='speed' value='10'></applet>

mcqs.explanation: Parameters go INSIDE the <applet> tag as <param> child elements: <applet code='App.class' width=300 height=300><param name='speed' value='10'><param name='color' value='red'></applet>. In Java: getParameter("speed") returns "10".

mcqs.question: What is the CODEBASE attribute of the <applet> tag used for?

options.B: Specifies the directory (URL) where the applet's .class files are located, if different from the HTML page's directory

mcqs.explanation: codebase='http://example.com/applets/' tells the browser to look for the .class files in the /applets/ directory. Without codebase, the browser looks in the same directory as the HTML file. Useful when class files are in a different location than the HTML page.

mcqs.question: What is the ARCHIVE attribute in the <applet> tag?

options.A: Archives the applet for later use
options.B: Specifies a JAR file containing the applet's classes, reducing download time by fetching one compressed file instead of multiple .class files

mcqs.explanation: archive='myapplet.jar' tells the browser to download the JAR (Java Archive) containing all class files and resources in one compressed download. This is much faster than downloading each .class separately, especially for applets with many classes.

mcqs.question: What is the ALT attribute in the <applet> tag?

options.B: Provides alternative text displayed if the browser cannot run the applet (Java not installed, disabled)

mcqs.explanation: alt='This applet requires Java' displays this text if the browser can't load the Java plugin or if Java is disabled. This is important for accessibility and user feedback — without alt, users with no Java see a blank area with no explanation.

mcqs.question: How does changing the width/height in the HTML <applet> tag affect the applet?

options.B: Changes the display area size without recompilation — the applet's getWidth()/getHeight() return the new values

mcqs.explanation: Width and height are HTML attributes, not Java code. Changing them in the HTML file immediately changes the applet's display size. The Java code reads these via getWidth()/getHeight(). No recompilation needed — just save the HTML and reload the page/appletviewer.

mcqs.question: What does the <title> tag inside <head> control?

options.A: The font size of the page
options.B: The text displayed in the browser's title bar or tab

mcqs.explanation: <title>My Page</title> inside <head> sets the browser tab/title bar text. When the appletviewer opens, this title appears in the viewer window's title bar. It doesn't appear in the page body itself.

mcqs.question: What is the ALIGN attribute in the <applet> tag?

options.B: Controls how the applet is positioned relative to surrounding text (left, right, top, bottom, middle)
options.C: Sets text alignment inside the applet

mcqs.explanation: align='left' positions the applet to the left with text flowing around it. Other values: right, top, bottom, middle, texttop. This controls the applet's layout within the HTML page, similar to how images are positioned with text.

mcqs.question: What does HSPACE and VSPACE in the <applet> tag control?

options.B: Horizontal and vertical spacing (padding) around the applet in pixels

mcqs.explanation: hspace='10' vspace='20' adds 10 pixels of horizontal padding and 20 pixels of vertical padding around the applet. This creates space between the applet and surrounding HTML content, improving visual separation.

mcqs.question: What is the NAME attribute in the <applet> tag used for?

options.B: Names the applet for inter-applet communication — getAppletContext().getApplet("name") retrieves it

mcqs.explanation: <applet name='calculator' code='Calc.class' ...> gives the applet a name. Other applets on the same page can find it: Applet calc = getAppletContext().getApplet("calculator"); This enables inter-applet communication — one applet can call methods on another.

mcqs.question: Why must the <applet> tag go inside the <body> tag?

options.B: The applet is visual content that belongs in the page body, not in the head (which is for metadata only)

mcqs.explanation: <head> contains metadata (title, meta tags, links). <body> contains visible page content. Since an applet is visible content, it belongs in <body>. Putting it in <head> is invalid HTML — browsers may ignore or misplace it.

mcqs.question: Why was the <applet> tag deprecated in HTML 4.01 and removed in HTML5?

options.B: Security risks from executing downloaded Java code in browsers led to the removal of NPAPI plugin support and the <applet> tag in modern HTML standards

mcqs.explanation: HTML 4.01 deprecated <applet> in favor of <object>. HTML5 removed <applet> entirely. The real reason: browsers (Chrome 2015, Firefox 2016, Edge 2017) dropped NPAPI Java plugin support due to repeated security vulnerabilities. Modern web development uses HTML5 Canvas, WebGL, and JavaScript instead of Java applets.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between <applet> and <object> tags for embedding Java?

options.B: <applet> is Java-specific (deprecated); <object> is a general-purpose embedding tag that can embed Java, Flash, PDF, etc., with type='application/x-java-applet'

mcqs.explanation: <object classid='clsid:...' type='application/x-java-applet'> is the HTML 4 standard for embedding any plugin content, including Java. <applet> was Java-specific and simpler but deprecated. <object> is more generic (embeds Flash, PDF, ActiveX) but more complex syntax. Both are now obsolete for Java in modern browsers.

mcqs.question: What is the MAYSCRIPT attribute in the <applet> tag and what does it enable?

options.B: Grants the applet permission to call JavaScript functions in the browser via the netscape.javascript.JSObject API

mcqs.explanation: <applet code='App.class' MAYSCRIPT ...> allows the applet to call JavaScript: JSObject window = JSObject.getWindow(this); window.eval("alert('Hello from Java!')"). Without MAYSCRIPT, calling JavaScript from the applet throws a security exception. This enabled Java-JavaScript interop for rich web integration.

mcqs.question: How does the browser's class loading mechanism for applets differ from standard Java class loading?

options.B: Browsers use a custom ClassLoader that loads classes from the network (via HTTP from codebase URL) instead of the local classpath, with security restrictions
options.D: Browsers use the same classpath as 'java' command

mcqs.explanation: Applet class loading: the browser provides a network ClassLoader that fetches .class files (and JARs) via HTTP from the codebase URL. This ClassLoader enforces the applet security sandbox (no local file access, restricted network). This is fundamentally different from 'java MyApp' which uses the local classpath with no restrictions.

mcqs.question: What is the 'same-origin policy' for applets and how does it relate to getCodeBase()?

options.A: Applets can connect to any server
options.B: Applets can only make network connections back to the host they were loaded from (getCodeBase().getHost()), preventing cross-origin data exfiltration
options.C: Same-origin means all applets share data

mcqs.explanation: Security: an applet loaded from http://example.com/applets/App.class can only open sockets/URLs to example.com. This prevents: 1) malicious applets scanning internal networks, 2) exfiltrating data to attacker servers, 3) acting as unauthorized proxies. getCodeBase().getHost() identifies the trusted origin. Signed applets can request overriding this.

mcqs.question: How does the <param> tag support applet customization without recompilation?

options.B: Parameters passed via <param> are read at runtime by getParameter() — changing HTML parameters customizes applet behavior without touching Java code

mcqs.explanation: HTML: <param name='bgcolor' value='FF0000'>. Java: String bg = getParameter('bgcolor'); setBackground(new Color(Integer.parseInt(bg, 16))). Changing the HTML param from 'FF0000' (red) to '00FF00' (green) changes the applet's background without recompiling. This is applet customization via configuration — powerful for reusable applets.

mcqs.question: What is the significance of the <object> tag with 'classid' vs 'type' for embedding Java?

options.B: classid specifies the exact implementation (ActiveX CLSID on Windows IE); type specifies the MIME type (application/x-java-applet) for cross-browser plugin detection

mcqs.explanation: IE used classid='clsid:8AD9C840-044E-11D1-B3E9-00805F499D93' (ActiveX CLSID for Java plugin). Other browsers used type='application/x-java-applet' (MIME type for plugin detection). Cross-browser HTML needed both: <object classid='...' type='...'>. This complexity was another reason applets fell out of favor.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, what is the purpose of showing different HTML tags (h1, b, i, a, img)?

options.B: To show that HTML pages can contain rich content alongside the applet — text, images, links — and the applet is just one embedded element within this larger page context
options.D: To show HTML is better than Java

mcqs.explanation: The demo shows that an applet is embedded within a full HTML page that also contains headings, formatted text, images, and links. The applet occupies a rectangular area defined by width/height, while the rest of the page contains standard HTML content. This contextualizes applets as one component of a larger web page.

mcqs.question: What is the practical impact of the browser removing Java plugin support on applet-based web applications?

options.B: All applet-based web applications stopped working in modern browsers, requiring migration to HTML5/JavaScript equivalents

mcqs.explanation: Chrome removed NPAPI (Java plugin) in 2015; Firefox in 2016; Edge never supported it. By 2017, ~95% of browsers couldn't run applets. Organizations with applet-based systems had to: rewrite UIs in JavaScript/HTML5, use browser extensions, or run applets in standalone appletviewer. This was a massive migration effort for enterprise Java web apps.

mcqs.question: From an architectural perspective, what was the fundamental security flaw in the applet model that led to its demise?

options.B: Executing arbitrary downloaded code (from a URL) on the user's machine, even in a sandbox, presented an ever-expanding attack surface — sandbox escapes were repeatedly found, making browser plugins fundamentally insecure

mcqs.explanation: The core issue: running third-party compiled code (Java bytecode) in the browser. Despite the sandbox, sandbox escape vulnerabilities were found regularly (Java zero-days). Each fix led to new escapes. Browser vendors concluded that executing downloaded native/plugin code is fundamentally more dangerous than sandboxed JavaScript. This insight drove the move to pure JavaScript + HTML5 — no plugins, no native code execution, just interpreted JavaScript in a V8-level sandbox.
